**Race Preview and Analysis**

The Stockholm Diamond League 200m on 7 June 2026 brings together a fascinating mix of proven championship medalists, a rising African star, a former 19.63 performer, and a young Swedish talent with home-track advantage. The form guide from the 2025 and early 2026 seasons strongly points toward Kenneth Bednarek as the favorite, but the battle behind him should be razor-sharp.

**Kenneth Bednarek** arrives as the man to beat. At 27, he is in his absolute prime, having won Olympic and World silver medals in the 200m. His 2025 season was exceptional: a 19.58 PB at the World Championships in Tokyo to take silver behind Letsile Tebogo, and a 19.67 at USAs in a stacked field. He has already shown superb early-2026 form, winning the Rabat Diamond League 200m on 31 May in **19.69 (+0.4)** — a time that is comfortably the fastest any man in this field has run this year. Bednarek’s 100m speed is also elite (9.79 in 2025), which allows him to carry immense momentum into the curve and hold off challenges down the straight. His consistency at the highest level, combined with that Rabat result just one week ago, makes him a clear frontrunner.

**Sinesipho Dambile** is the most intriguing threat. The 23-year-old South African has made a massive leap in 2026. His breakthrough came in Nairobi on 24 April, where he ran **19.77 (+0.3)** — a lifetime best that places him firmly in the global elite. He then backed that up with a 20.03 (+0.4) in Rabat on 31 May, finishing third behind Bednarek and just outside his Nairobi form. Dambile’s 2025 included a 19.97 semi-final at the Tokyo World Championships, showing he can produce under pressure. He has the youth and upward trajectory to challenge for second here. His ability to run a fast, controlled bend and finish strongly suggests he can dip under 20.00 again in Stockholm, especially if he can stay within striking distance of Bednarek off the turn.

**Reynier Mena** is a fascinating wildcard. At 29, the Cuban owns a 19.63 PB from 2022, which ties him with Xavier Carter for #12 on the all-time list. However, his recent form has been inconsistent. He won the 2025 Stockholm meeting in **20.05 (+2.0)** , but that was a wind-aided, race-fast time on the same track. In 2026, his best is 20.15 in Savona (20 May) and 20.35 in Savona two weeks later, a slight regression from his peak. Mena’s indoor season was solid but unspectacular, and his 2025 Diamond League final in Zurich was only 20.26. He is a proven big-race performer, but at 29, he may be past his absolute peak. He has the raw talent to challenge for the podium, but his 2026 form is not screaming 19.8-low. Expect a competitive 20.0-high, good enough for third if Dambile slips, but likely outpaced by the younger South African.

**Courtney Lindsey** is difficult to read. At 27, he has outstanding credentials: a 19.82 at the 2025 US Championships (4th) and a 19.87 in the Prefontaine Classic. However, his 2026 season has been sluggish by his standards. He ran 20.28 (-1.3) in Tokyo on 17 May, and then a disappointing **20.21 (+0.4)** in Rabat on 31 May, finishing 7th. That Rabat performance is a red flag — he was beaten by both Dambile and Traore, and looked heavy-legged. Lindsey is a powerful sprinter with sub-10 100m speed, but his 200m rhythm has not clicked this year. He might bounce back in Stockholm, but the data suggests he is a step behind the top three right now. He will be in the mix for 4th, but 20.15 feels like his ceiling on current form.

**Cheickna Traore**, the 25-year-old Ivorian, is a fascinating figure. He just won the 2026 African Championships 200m title in Accra (20.32 wind-legal) and set a national record in 2024. In Rabat on 31 May, he ran **20.15 (+0.4)** to finish 4th, ahead of Lindsey and Mena. That is his best outdoor 200m of the season and suggests he is improving. Traore has good top-end speed and a strong finish, as shown in his 10.16 100m earlier this spring. He lacks the championship medal pedigree of the top names, but he is clearly a rising force. He could challenge for 4th if Lindsey struggles again, and his 20.15 in Rabat indicates he is capable of a similar time here. 5th is a fair prediction, but he has upside.

**Jeremiah Azu** is a superb 100m and indoor sprinter — 2025 World and European Indoor 60m champion — but the 200m is not his primary event. At 24, his best 200m outdoor times this season are modest: 20.73 (+1.6) in Belfast on 9 May. He has some experience over the distance — including a 20.77 indoor win — but his lack of a 200m outdoor breakthrough this year is telling. Azu is quick off the line and could run a decent bend, but he will likely fade against specialists in the final 50 metres. He will be competitive for the home straight, but a time in the low 20.7s feels realistic. He will not threaten the podium but should beat the local Swede.

**Erik Erlandsson**, at 21, is the young Swedish hope. He is a superb indoor 200m runner, holding the Swedish indoor record, but his outdoor 200m results are shallower. His best outdoors in 2025 was 20.57 (+2.0) at this very meeting last year. In 2026, he has run only indoor races (20.90 best). He is talented and will have home support, but he is still developing and likely a year or two away from truly competing at Diamond League level. A time in the 20.7s or low 20.8s is probable, and he will likely finish last in this elite field. The experience will be valuable for him.

**Head-to-Head Comparisons**

- **Bednarek vs. Dambile vs. Mena:** In Rabat on 31 May, Bednarek (19.69) beat Dambile (20.03) by 0.34, and Mena was not in that race. However, Dambile's 19.77 in Nairobi is significantly faster than Mena's 2026 best of 20.15. Dambile also ran 20.03 in Rabat, which suggests he is 0.10-0.12 ahead of Mena on current form. Bednarek’s 19.69 in Rabat is a full 0.34 faster than Dambile’s best this year — a clear gap.
- **Lindsey vs. Traore:** They met in Rabat, with Traore (20.15) beating Lindsey (20.21) by 0.06. That was a direct head-to-head. Lindsey’s 2026 best is 20.28, while Traore’s is 20.15. Traore has the edge.
- **Azu vs. Erlandsson:** No direct head-to-head, but Azu’s 20.73 in Belfast is faster than Erlandsson’s 20.57 outdoor best (wind-aided) from 2025. On a calm day, Azu should be quicker, but Erlandsson’s home track might spur him to a season's best.

**Key Factors**

- **Track:** Stockholm’s Olympiastadion produces fast times. The 2025 men’s 200m was won in 20.05 (+2.0), and the conditions should be fair.
- **Form:** Bednarek is the only man who has broken 19.8 this year. Dambile has broken 19.8. Everyone else is 20.0 or slower.
- **Motivation:** Erlandsson will have the crowd behind him, but that rarely makes a 0.3-second difference. Azu is a 100m specialist testing his range. Lindsey needs a rebound after a poor Rabat.

**Conclusion**

Kenneth Bednarek is a near-certain winner given his 19.69 in Rabat just last week. Sinesipho Dambile has the form and youth to take second with a 19.95, continuing his meteoric rise. Reynier Mena is a classy veteran but his 2026 times do not match his 2022 peak, so he settles for third. Courtney Lindsey looks off-form and will fight with Cheickna Traore for 4th, with Traore getting the nod based on their Rabat clash. Jeremiah Azu and Erik Erlandsson round out the field, both respectful but not in medal contention. Expect a fast, clean race with Bednarek controlling the bend and holding off Dambile down the home straight.

### Race Preview & Reasoning

**The Inevitable Favorite: Keely Hodgkinson**  
At just 23, Hodgkinson is the reigning Olympic and World Indoor champion, and her 2025–26 form is terrifying. Her 1:54.74 in Silesia (Aug 2025) is the fastest time in this field by nearly a full second, and her indoor 1:54.87 in Liévin (Feb 2026) proves she’s carrying that speed into the new season. She also ran 51.49 over 400m indoors in March, demonstrating raw leg speed that no one here can match. Even her “disappointing” bronze at the 2025 World Championships (1:54.91) was a world-class mark. On the Stockholm track, where she won the 2023 edition, she will sit near the front, control the pace, and unleash her trademark kick over the final 150m. Expect a controlled 1:56-mid, not a personal best, but enough to dominate.

**The Rising Threat: Audrey Werro**  
The 21-year-old Swiss star is on a trajectory that mirrors a young Hodgkinson. Her 1:55.91 win in Zürich (Aug 2025) and 1:56.29 national title showed she can run sub-1:57 under pressure. Crucially, her 1:56.56 victory in Rabat (31 May 2026 – just a week before this race) was a dominant front-running effort against many of the same athletes (Bourgoin, Sekgodiso, Getachew). Her indoor silver at the 2026 World Indoors (1:56.64) behind Hodgkinson (1:55.30) confirms she is the clear No. 2. Werro’s only weakness is a tendency to fade slightly in the final 50m against top-tier closers, but her early-season confidence and Rabat win suggest she’ll push Hodgkinson to the line.

**The American Surge: Roisin Willis & Sage Hurta-Klecker**  
Willis, the 21-year-old US champion (1:59.26 at the 2025 USAs) and NCAA champion (1:58.13), has the most upside in this field after the top two. Her 1:58.08 win at the LA Track Festival (23 May 2026) showed she’s rounding into peak outdoor form. She has a potent kick (indoor 600m PB of 1:24.87) and thrives in tactical races. However, she lacks experience at the very front of a Diamond League pace; she tends to win from behind. In Stockholm, she may get boxed in early. Still, her raw strength places her third.

Hurta-Klecker (27) is the savvy veteran, with a 1:55.89 fifth-place finish at the 2025 World Championships – the best championship finish among the Americans here. Her 1:58.18 in Rabat (31 May) was a solid tune-up, though she faded to 8th. Her consistency is underrated, but she lacks the top-end closing speed of Willis. She’ll push the pace early to try to break the field, but expect her to settle for 4th.

**The Battle for Mid-Pack: Sekgodiso, Bourgoin, Reekie**  
Prudence Sekgodiso (23) is the reigning World Indoor champion (1:58.40) but has been erratic outdoors. Her 1:57.16 in Eugene (July 2025) is excellent, but she also DNF’d at the 2025 World Championships heats – a mental red flag. Her 1:57.41 in Rabat (6th) is a season’s best but behind Werro. She has the talent to challenge for 3rd, but her inconsistency and tendency to run aggressive first laps often leave her vulnerable over the final 100m.

Anaïs Bourgoin (29) is a late bloomer who ran 1:56.97 in Zürich (2025) and placed 3rd in the World Championships semi. She’s tactically smart and rarely runs a bad race, but she doesn’t have a gear under 1:57. Her 1:57.39 in Rabat (5th) suggests she’s stuck in the 1:57-low range. Expect her to be in the mix until 600m, then fall off.

Jemma Reekie (27) is a curious case: she’s the former British No. 2 who has focused on the 1500m in 2025–26 (4:02.14 indoor 1500m) but has struggled to recapture her 2020–21 800m form. Her 1:58.66 in Stockholm last year (5th) and a DNF in Bydgoszcz in May 2026 are worrying. She has the speed (51.49 over 400m indoors in 2022) but lacks race sharpness over two laps. 7th seems generous; she could slip lower if the pace is hot.

**The Tail-End Contenders**  
Nigist Getachew (23) is a strong indoor athlete (indoor Worlds silver in 1:59.63) but hasn’t translated that to outdoor success – her 1:58.58 in Rabat (11th) was well off the pace. She runs best from the front but lacks the durability to hold off stronger closers.

Anna Wielgosz (32) is the European Indoor champion (2:02.09) but is clearly past her peak. She DNF’d in her last 800m in May 2026 and rarely dips below 1:58 outdoors.

Gabriela Gajanová (26) had a breakthrough indoor season (1:59.85 in Toruń) but her outdoor times are pedestrian (2:03.87 in Bydgoszcz, May 2026). She’s a 2:00-low runner at best.

Raevyn Rogers (29) is a former Olympic bronze medalist, but at 29, her best days are behind her. Her 1:59.82 in LA (May 2026) was a distant 3rd behind Willis. She’s running for pride but lacks speed.

Rachel Klopfenstein (30) is a solid 2:00-flat runner (1:59.79 in May 2026) but is competing for Mauritius after a nationality change. She’s outclassed in this field and will likely serve as a pace-sitter before fading.

**Tactical Summary**  
Hodgkinson will lead from the front or sit just off the pace – her preference is to avoid early congestion. Werro will shadow her closely. The pack will be tight through 400m (projected 57–58s), then the real racing begins at 600m. Hodgkinson’s kick is unmatched; Werro will close hard but settle for silver. Willis and Hurta-Klecker will duel for 3rd, with Willis’s youth and kick giving her the edge. The rest will fight for placings, with times ranging from 1:57 to 2:00 depending on how the race breaks. It won’t be a record-setting performance, but it will be a tactical masterclass from the Olympic champion.

**Top Tier (1–4)**  
The race revolves around the Rabat Diamond League just one week earlier (31 May 2026). **Yared Nuguse** won there in 3:30.35, demonstrating sharp form after a consistent indoor/road season (including a 3:54.06 road mile in April). His North American mile record and Olympic bronze pedigree make him the clear favourite; he thrives in fast, tactical Diamond League fields. **Azeddine Habz** trailed Nuguse by 0.33s in Rabat (3:30.68) and boasts a 3:27.49 personal best from Paris 2025. **Contenders (5–8)**  
**Narve Gilje Nordås** has a solid 3:32.52 win in Rehlingen (May 24) and a 3:33.45 in Rabat—modest compared to his 3:30.26 from 2025. He is still learning, but his indoor 3:33.96 in Liévin shows he belongs. **Robert Farken** has not contested a 1500m in 2026 outdoor, but his 2:17.17 1000m in Dresden (May 31) indicates speed. His 3:33.47 indoor in Toruń and previous 3:31.15 in Zürich suggest he can rebound, but consistency remains an issue.

**Veterans and Distance Specialists (9–16)**  
**Timothy Cheruiyot** has looked off all season. His best 1500m in 2026 is a 3:38.16 in Nairobi (April), and he has been running 3000m/5000m instead. At 30, the former world champion may be transitioning to longer events; Stockholm could be a testing ground. **Nico Young**, primarily a 5000m/10,000m runner, ran 3:34.56 in Los Angeles (May 23). He has the endurance to stay in touch but lacks the specific speed. **Jake Heyward** has only two 1500m races in 2026, the best 3:34.18 (May 9). The Welshman is a European silver medallist but has been injury‑prone. **Jochem Vermeulen** hasn’t raced outdoors in 2026; his indoor 3:33.71 from Liévin is promising but unproven. **Hobbs Kessler** is a major question mark: after a DNF in the 1500m at the LA Track Festival (May 23) and a 1:46.04 800m, his recent form is poor. **Race Dynamics**  
A pacelight will likely target 2:50 through 1200m (≈3:33 pace) before a furious last lap. Nuguse’s Rabat win—where he closed in 53.0—makes him the man to beat. Habz will sit on his shoulder, while Myers may try to inject pace earlier. Cheruiyot and Kessler are wild cards, but neither has shown enough to crack the top five. The Stockholm crowd will roar for Pihlström and Almgren, but their best chances are in longer events. Expect a sub‑3:30 winner and a deep field finishing within two seconds of the lead.

### Reasoning

**1. Valarie Sion** – The two-time Olympic champion and reigning World champion (Tokyo 2025) is in a league of her own. Her 2026 season already includes a 73.10 m throw (Oklahoma, April) and back‑to‑back Diamond League wins in Xiamen (68.45 m) and Rabat (68.75 m). Sion has won every outdoor discus final she has contested since 2022, and her consistency over 68 m even on slightly off days makes her the clear favorite. Stockholm’s atmosphere will not rattle her; expect another comfortable victory near 69.5 m.

**2. Jorinde van Klinken** – The Dutch record holder (70.99 m) has emerged as Sion’s primary rival this year. She finished 2nd in Rabat (66.72 m) and 3rd in Xiamen (64.27 m) – the latter a rare misstep. Van Klinken also threw 68.98 m in Oklahoma (April) and 70.99 m in the same meet, showing she can peak when the field pushes her. She out‑threw Tausaga and Jackson at the World Championships (silver, 67.50 m) and has the technique to consistently hit 66‑67 m. In Stockholm she will again be the clear second force.

**3. Laulauga Tausaga** – The 2023 World champion has been inconsistent in 2026. Her best this year is 65.94 m (3rd in Rabat), down from her 70.72 m personal best set in 2025. However, she remains a championship performer – 6th at the 2025 Worlds (65.49 m) but with a 70.72 m peak that proves her ceiling. Tausaga has a tendency to struggle on the European circuit (8th in Rome 2025, 8th in Stockholm 2025), but her recent Rabat mark was solid. She should edge out the younger Jackson thanks to superior experience and a stronger overall résumé.

**4. Cierra Jackson** – The 2025 NCAA champion has made an impressive transition to the professional ranks. In 2026 she has thrown 67.25 m (4th in Oklahoma) and 65.79 m (4th in Rabat), and she already beat Tausaga head‑to‑head in Rabat by 0.15 m. Jackson’s youth and rapid improvement (65.82 m NCAA title, 67.82 m at Prefontaine 2025) suggest she is closing the gap. However, her peak marks have come in early season US meets; the European travel and pressure of a Diamond League may still see her lag slightly behind the more seasoned Tausaga. Still, a 66‑m barrier is likely.

**5. Bin Feng** – The Chinese thrower and 2024 Olympic silver medalist is a model of consistency. Her 2026 season includes 65.03 m (2nd in Xiamen) and 64.51 m (5th in Rabat). Feng’s best recent mark of 69.12 m came in 2022, but she has not reached 67 m in the last two years. Her reliable 64‑65 m range keeps her in the mix, but she lacks the firepower to challenge the top three. She will need a near‑perfect throw to surpass Jackson, but her steady technique should secure fifth ahead of the Germans.

**6. Shanice Craft** – The German veteran (32) has a personal best of 66.65 m from 2025 and opened 2026 with 66.03 m in Magdeburg. However, she has faded in the most recent Diamond League stops: 6th in Xiamen (63.96 m) and 7th in Rabat (62.59 m). Craft’s age and a slightly inconsistent release may limit her to the mid‑64 m range. She is still capable of beating her younger compatriot Steinacker on a good day, but her recent results suggest she is not in top form.

**7. Marike Steinacker** – Another German, 33 years old, Steinacker threw her season’s best of 66.55 m in April (Oklahoma) but has been unable to replicate that in high‑level competition. She finished 9th in Rabat (61.84 m) and has not placed higher than 5th in a Diamond League since 2023. Her technique is solid, and she can hit 64‑65 m on home soil, but in Stockholm she will likely settle for mid‑63 m unless the conditions are perfect.

**8. Vanessa Kamga** – The Swedish home favorite will have crowd support, but her 2026 form has been erratic. She threw 64.02 m in Xiamen (5th) but collapsed to 59.78 m in Rabat (11th). Kamga’s personal best of 66.61 m came at the 2025 World Championships, where she placed 4th, but she has not shown that level consistently. A modest bounce to 62‑63 m is possible, but she is unlikely to challenge the stronger field.

**9. Silinda Moráles** – The Cuban and 2025 World bronze medalist (67.25 m) has had a terrible 2026 campaign. She could only manage 59.07 m in Xiamen (10th) and has not competed in Rabat. Her early‑season domestic meets in Cuba were all around 62‑63 m, far below her peak. The transition to European competition has exposed technical issues. Unless she rediscovers her form dramatically, she will struggle to break 61 m.
blurbs.Pole vault, Men:
**Predicted Finish – Men's Pole Vault, Stockholm Diamond League (7 June 2026)**

1. **Armand Duplantis (SWE)** – 6.23 m  
2. **Kurtis Marschall (AUS)** – 6.01 m  
3. **Sondre Guttormsen (NOR)** – 5.97 m  
4. **Zachery Bradford (USA)** – 5.86 m  
5. **Sam Kendricks (USA)** – 5.82 m  
6. **Menno Vloon (NED)** – 5.78 m  
7. **Thibaut Collet (FRA)** – 5.74 m  
8. **Renaud Lavillenie (FRA)** – 5.66 m  
9. **Baptiste Thiery (FRA)** – 5.60 m  

---

### Preview and Reasoning

#### 1. Armand Duplantis – The Inevitable Champion
Duplantis enters Stockholm on a trajectory that borders on mythological. At 26, he has already won nine senior global titles, holds the world record at 6.31 m (set indoors in March 2026), and has been utterly dominant in every competition he has entered since 2020. His 2025 outdoor season included a 6.28 m clearance in this very stadium (BAUHAUS-Galan, June 2025) and a 6.30 m to win the World Championships in Tokyo. In 2026, he has only competed once outdoors so far—a 6.12 m victory in Shaoxing in mid-May—but his indoor form was staggering: 6.31 m in Uppsala, 6.25 m at the World Indoor Championships in Toruń. The Stockholm crowd will lift him, the conditions at Olympiastadion are historically favorable for him, and he will likely attempt a world record after securing the win. A predicted 6.23 m reflects a conservative outdoor opener in front of a home crowd where he will likely go for height rather than risk injury chasing 6.30+ in early June.

#### 2. Kurtis Marschall – The Reliable Contender
Marschall has quietly become the most consistent non-Duplantis vaulter in the world. His bronze at the 2025 World Championships (5.95 m) was no fluke—he backed it up with a 6.00 m indoor clearance at the All Star Perche in February 2026 and another 6.00 m at the World Indoor Championships in Toruń (third place). His 2025 outdoor season featured a 5.93 m in Athens and a 5.92 m in Monaco, and he finished second in last year's Stockholm Diamond League with 5.90 m. Crucially, he has shown he can rise to 6.00 m when the moment demands it. His start to 2026 outdoors (5.80 m in Shaoxing, second behind Duplantis) suggests he is building form. He has the technique and nerve to push the bar to 6.01 m in Stockholm, especially if the conditions are good and Duplantis draws the field higher.

#### 3. Sondre Guttormsen – The Breakout Star
Guttormsen has been the revelation of the 2026 indoor season. He jumped 6.06 m indoors in Rouen (March 2026)—a massive personal best and just 0.05 m off Duplantis’s indoor world record at the time. He followed that with 6.00 m in Uppsala and a fourth-place finish at the World Indoor Championships (5.95 m). While he has historically struggled to translate indoor momentum to outdoor success (his 2025 outdoor best was only 5.80 m), his confidence is at an all-time high. He also has raw speed and power that suit the Stockholm runway. If he can channel his indoor form, 5.97 m is realistic. He is the biggest threat to Marschall for second place, but his relative lack of outdoor consistency at 5.90+ meters pushes him to third for now.

#### 4. Zachery Bradford – High Ceiling, Inconsistent Floor
Bradford has some of the best indoor marks in the world over the past year: 6.01 m to win USATF Indoor in February 2026, plus multiple 5.90 m clearances indoors. However, his outdoor record is troubling. He has not cleared 5.80 m outdoors since 2019, and his 2025 outdoor season was a disaster: no-heights in Ann Arbor, Tucson, Innsbruck, and only 5.52 m at his best. His 2026 outdoor debut in Shaoxing was a disappointing 5.60 m for ninth place. The raw talent is undeniable, but he has not proven he can reliably produce on the Diamond League outdoor circuit. Stockholm could be his breakthrough, or it could be another frustrating night. I predict a moderate but solid 5.86 m—enough for fourth given the quality of the field below him, but not yet a podium threat.

#### 5. Sam Kendricks – The Veteran Fighting Decline
At 33, Kendricks is no longer the world-beater who won gold in 2017 and 2019. His 2025 was a mixed bag: a fourth-place finish at the World Championships (5.95 m) showed he can still peak for majors, but his Diamond League performances were often subdued (5.62 m in Oslo, 5.60 m in Stockholm, 5.82 m in Monaco). His 2026 indoor season was similarly inconsistent—a 5.90 m in Uppsala was his best, but he also had a 5.70 m in Rouen and a 5.60 m at Liévin. His outdoor form in 2026 has been unremarkable: 5.70 m in Shaoxing and 5.60 m in Turku. The motivation is still there, but the margins have shrunk. He will fight for a top-five finish, but he is no longer a safe bet to clear 5.90 m. A 5.82 m prediction reflects a gritty, experienced performance that might have been fifth or sixth a few years ago.

#### 6. Menno Vloon – The Steady Dutchman
Vloon is a model of consistency in the 5.70–5.85 m range. He won the European Indoor title in 2025, cleared 5.90 m at the World Championships in Tokyo (seventh), and has hit 5.85 m indoors in 2026. His outdoor consistency is impressive: 5.82 m in Xiamen, 5.82 m in Shaoxing, 5.80 m in Stockholm last year. However, he rarely threatens 6.00 m and tends to plateau once the bar goes above 5.90 m. He is reliable for a mid-field finish but lacks the extra gear to challenge for the podium. I expect 5.78 m—a solid, professional clearance that keeps him in the Diamond League points hunt.

#### 7. Thibaut Collet – The Plateauing Frenchman
Collet has a personal best of 5.95 m outdoors, but he has not approached that since 2024. His 2025 season featured a 5.90 m at the Mondo Classic indoors and a 5.90 m at the World Championships (fifth place), but his outdoor Diamond League marks were mostly in the 5.55–5.75 m range. In 2026, he has been stuck around 5.70–5.85 m indoors and has not yet broken 5.75 m outdoors. The talent is there, but he seems to have stalled. Stockholm is a chance to prove he can still improve, but the data suggests a 5.74 m finish—competitive but not exceptional.

#### 8. Renaud Lavillenie – The Legend Fading
At 39, Lavillenie is competing on heart and history. His 2025 season included a few solid 5.82 m clearances (French Championships, Monaco, Lausanne), but he also had no-heights in Eugene and Zürich and finished only eighth at the World Championships. His 2026 has been grim: a 5.50 m in Duszniki in May suggests the end may be near. The Olympic gold medalist and former world record holder deserves immense respect, but the numbers do not lie. He will likely exit around 5.66 m—a valiant effort from a champion who refuses to quit, but he is no longer a factor in the top half of a Diamond League field.

#### 9. Baptiste Thiery – The Youngster Learning
Thiery is only 24 and has shown flashes indoors (5.91 m in 2025, 5.90 m in 2026), but his outdoor results have not yet matched. He has no outdoor mark above 5.76 m over the past two years, and his 2025 outdoor season was inconsistent (5.53 m in Athens, 5.40 m at French Championships). He is clearly talented but still raw. Stockholm will be a learning experience. A 5.60 m clearance would be a reasonable step forward on the Diamond League stage.

---

### Key Matchups to Watch
- **Duplantis vs. the World Record**: If the weather holds, expect him to raise the bar to 6.32 m or 6.33 m after securing the win.  
- **Marschall vs. Guttormsen**: This is the real battle for second place. Marschall’s experience and 6.00 m credentials give him the edge, but Guttormsen’s indoor 6.06 m suggests he could spring a surprise.  
- **Bradford’s Outdoor Test**: Can he finally replicate his indoor success on grass? A top-four finish in Stockholm would be a significant career milestone.  
- **Kendricks’s Last Stand**: The American is running out of time to reclaim past glory. A 5.90 m+ clearance here would signal he is still dangerous.  

The Stockholm Diamond League men’s pole vault will once again be a showcase for Duplantis’s genius, but the depth of the field—with Marschall, Guttormsen, and even a resurgent Bradford—ensures that every clearance from 5.80 m upward will be fiercely contested.

### Preview and Analysis

**The Favourite: Marwa Bouzayani**  
Bouzayani arrives in Stockholm as the form athlete of the field. Her recent steeplechase performances in China are exceptional: 8:58.09 in Shaoxing (3rd) and 8:59.25 in Xiamen (4th) – both in high-quality Diamond League races. She also placed 4th in the World Championships final in Tokyo 2025 (9:01.46), demonstrating her ability to perform under pressure. At 28, she is in her prime, and her consistency across multiple surfaces (road, indoor, cross country) shows excellent stamina and tactical versatility. Expect her to control the race from the front and push for a sub-9:00 clocking.

**The Veteran Challenger: Alice Finot**  
The French European champion and record holder is 34 but remains a formidable competitor. Her 2025 season included a solid 9:09.84 in Eugene and she won the French title. However, her 2026 campaign has been quiet – no steeplechase results since mid-2025. She did run 32:57 for 10km in January, suggesting she has maintained fitness. Finot’s pedigree and kick are undeniable, but she may lack the race sharpness of Bouzayani. She will likely sit behind the Tunisian and attempt a late surge, but her best days may be just past. A time around 8:59 is a strong return.

**The Rising Brit: Elise Thorner**  
Thorner is the most improved athlete in the field. At 24, she won the UK title in 2025 and placed 11th in the World Championships final. Her 2026 form is outstanding: she won the LA Track Festival steeplechase on 23 May in 9:07.39, a personal best by a significant margin. She also ran 8:39.87 indoors for 3000m flat, indicating strong speed. Thorner has developed excellent barrier technique and tactical sense. She will challenge for the podium and could surprise if the pace slackens.

**The Ethiopian Young Guns: Alemnat Walle and Kena Tufa**  
Walle, just 19, already has a World Championships final appearance (though a DNF in the heats). In 2026, she ran 9:10.05 in Shaoxing (5th) and 9:15.79 in Xiamen (8th), then won in Turku on 3 June in 9:16.18. She is raw but talented. Kena Tufa (20) ran 8:59.66 in Shaoxing (4th) but faded to 9:11.36 in Xiamen (5th) and then ran a mediocre 4:09.59 over 1500m in Turku. Tufa’s inconsistency is a concern, but her 8:59 mark shows she can run with the best. Walle has better recent momentum and slightly greater reliability.

**The German Trio: Meyer, Krause, Gürth**  
Lea Meyer (28) is the most consistent German. She ran 9:09.21 in Oslo 2025 and 9:09.73 in Paris, and finished 12th in the World final. She also won the German 5000m title. However, she DNF’d in Lausanne and had a mixed 2026 so far (4th in Boston 5k, DNF in LA). She is capable of a sub-9:10 but lacks the top-end speed of the leaders. Gesa Felicitas Krause (33) is a former world medallist but has struggled with DNFs in recent seasons. Her 2025 World final was a respectable 9:14.27, and she has run well on the road (1:08:59 half marathon). She may not be a podium threat but can outrun younger rivals. Olivia Gürth (23) is still developing – she ran 9:15.28 in the World heats but has DNF’d in two of her last three steeplechases. She lacks consistency.

**The Americans: Halladay, Jennings, Wayment, Markezich**  
Lexy Halladay (24) is the clear leader of this group. She won the US title in 2025 (9:09.14) and has a strong indoor background (8:38.78 for 3000m). Her 2026 outdoor steeplechase marks (9:13.99 in Shaoxing, 9:14.96 in Xiamen) are steady but not elite. She has the speed to dip under 9:10 if the race is honest. Gabrielle Jennings (27) has a best of 9:06.61 from 2025 but has not run a steeplechase in 2026 until her 9:21.57 win in LA on 23 May – a promising return. She struggles in deep fields. Courtney Wayment (27) has had a poor 2026: 14th in Shaoxing (9:27.96) and 13th in Xiamen (9:29.51). She has not recovered her 2024 form and will be a shadow of her Olympic self. Olivia Markezich (25) has similar struggles: 11th and 16th in the Chinese meets. The American group outside Halladay is off form.

**The Scandinavians and Others**  
Ilona Mononen (FIN, 22) is the Finnish record holder and ran 9:18.50 in Turku on 3 June. She is improving rapidly and will have home support in Stockholm (though the race is in Sweden, a Finnish athlete often draws regional interest). Kinga Królik (POL, 26) has a best of 9:22.14 but struggled in 2026 (8th in Turku in 9:33.79). Wosane Asefa (ETH, 18) is a huge talent – she won the African U20 cross country and ran 9:20.83 in Hengelo in 2025, but her 2026 steeplechase marks are weaker (9:41.76 at African Championships). She may be better suited to longer distances. Meseret Yeshaneh (ETH, 20) has strong flat speed (8:56 indoor 3000m) but has not translated it to the barriers. Olivia Gürth and Agnieszka Chorzępa (POL) are likely to be outclassed.

**Race Dynamics**  
Expect Bouzayani to push the pace from the gun, aiming to break the field early. Finot and Thorner will sit in the top three, with Walle and Tufa trying to hang on. The pace will be honest – likely through 2000m in around 5:58, setting up a fast last kilometer. The barriers and water jump on Stockholm’s track (Olympiastadion) are standard, and the weather in early June should be mild. Bouzayani’s strength and recent form should prevail, with Finot using her kick to hold off Thorner. The young Ethiopians may fade, while Meyer and Halladay battle for the next spots. This will be the fastest race of the 2026 Diamond League season so far.

### **Reasoning**

The Stockholm Diamond League field is deep, but recent form – especially from the Shaoxing Diamond League on 16 May and the Paavo Nurmi Games on 3 June – provides the clearest head‑to‑head evidence.

**Winner – Monae’ Nichols (USA, 27)**  
Nichols has been the most consistent jumper in the world over the past month. She won the Shaoxing Diamond League with a solid **6.89 m** (–0.2 wind), then backed it up with **6.88 m** (+0.7) at the Paavo Nurmi Games just four days before Stockholm. She also jumped **6.85 m** indoors in February and recorded a wind‑legal **7.07 m** (+1.4) in April. No other athlete has matched her frequency of 6.85+ jumps in 2026. At 27, she is in her prime and thrives on the global stage – expect her to edge a narrow win.

**2nd – Malaika Mihambo (GER, 31)**  
The two‑time world champion and Olympic gold medalist is building nicely. After a quiet indoor season (best 6.57 m), she has improved outdoors: **6.82 m** on 24 May and **6.87 m** (+1.0) on 31 May. Her Tokyo 2025 silver medal (6.99 m) shows she can still produce top‑end leaps. However, she has not yet broken 6.90 this season, and at 31 she may be pacing herself. Stockholm will be her first Diamond League of 2026, and while she is a proven big‑meet performer, Nichols’ current momentum gives her a slight edge.

**3rd – Agate de Sousa (POR, 25)**  
De Sousa is the reigning World Indoor Champion (6.92 m in Toruń, March 2026) and has been outstanding indoors. Outdoors, she tied for second in Shaoxing with **6.78 m** (–0.1) and produced a wind‑legal 6.97 m indoors earlier. Her consistency (six meets at 6.78 or better this year) makes her a podium threat. She lacks the raw 7‑m firepower of the top two, but she rarely underperforms.

**4th – Natalia Linares (COL, 22)**  
Linares is the youngest in the top five and already a World Championships bronze medalist (2025) and World Indoor bronze medalist (2026). She also tied for second in Shaoxing with **6.78 m** (–0.1) – the same mark as de Sousa. Her outdoor best is 6.95 m (December 2025 in Lima), and she has a steep upward trajectory. She may lack the experience of the veterans, but her raw talent and fearlessness make her a threat to de Sousa on a good day.

**5th – Alexis Brown (USA, 24)**  
Brown looked sensational in April with a wind‑legal **7.07 m** (+1.4) at the Tom Jones Memorial. However, she struggled to replicate that in Shaoxing, placing third with **6.75 m** (+0.3) – a full 0.32 m off her best. She also ran the 100 m frequently this spring, which may have diluted her focus. At 24, she has huge potential, but her inconsistency (6.94 m NCAA win vs 6.63 m at the 2025 NCAA final) suggests she is still learning to handle top‑level Diamond League pressure. A 6.78–6.80 m jump is reasonable, but she is unlikely to match her early‑season peak.

**6th – Larissa Iapichino (ITA, 23)**  
The European Indoor Champion (2025) and World Indoor silver medalist (2026) has been slightly off her best outdoors. She managed only **6.69 m** (+0.1) in Shaoxing, well below her 7.06 m outdoor best from 2025. Indoors she was superb (6.93 m in January), but her outdoor rhythm has not clicked. At 23, she is still developing, but Stockholm comes at a time when she needs a confidence‑boosting jump. Expect a modest improvement to the 6.70–6.75 m range, but not enough to crack the top five.

**7th – Claire Bryant (USA, 24)**  
The 2025 World Indoor Champion (6.96 m) has been underwhelming outdoors in 2026. She placed fourth in Shaoxing (6.70 m) and fourth in Turku (6.60 m), with her best outdoor of the year being **6.75 m** indoors in January. She has not reached 6.80 m since her 2025 season (6.91 m in Warsaw). Her technique appears solid, but she lacks the explosive pop that pushed her to the indoor title. A 6.65–6.70 m jump is the likely outcome.

**8th – Khaddi Sagnia (SWE, 31)**  
Sagnia is a hometown favourite, but her recent form is a concern. Her best 2026 mark is **6.78 m** indoors (4th at World Indoors), but she has no outdoor results this season. In 2025 she struggled to break 6.55 m outdoors (best 6.69 m in Košice). At 31, she is past her prime (PB 6.95 m in 2022). The home crowd may lift her to 6.60–6.65 m, but she is not a medal contender.

**9th – Hilary Kpatcha (FRA, 27)**  
Kpatcha had a strong 2025 (7.02 m street jump, 4th at Worlds) but has stagnated in 2026. Her outdoor marks are mediocre: **6.56 m** (0.0) in Grenoble and **6.53 m** (–0.8) in Košice. She is clearly not in the same form as last year. A jump around 6.55–6.60 m seems probable, which will leave her near the bottom of this deep field.

**10th – Maja Åskag (SWE, 23)**  
Åskag is primarily a triple jumper (14.24 m in June) and only occasionally contests the long jump at the elite level. Her 2026 long jump season best is **6.59 m** indoors, and her only outdoor long jump this year was **6.45 m** (+1.6) at the Nordic Championships. Against a world‑class field, she will struggle to break 6.55 m. Her focus is clearly on the triple jump, and Stockholm is likely a secondary event for her.

**Competition Preview and Analysis**

The Stockholm Diamond League brings together the world’s elite discus throwers just four days after the Paavo Nurmi Games in Turku, where most of this field competed. That meeting provides the clearest recent head‑to‑head data, and it strongly influences the predicted order.

**Kristjan Čeh** arrives as the man to beat. The 26‑year‑old Slovenian world champion (2022) and silver medallist (2023) has been in imperious form. At the Paavo Nurmi Games on 3 June he threw **69.13 m** to win comfortably, and earlier this season he unleashed **70.58 m** to win in Shaoxing (16 May) and **72.61 m** at the Oklahoma Throws Series. Čeh’s consistency in the high‑69 to low‑70 range and his ability to deliver under pressure (he also won the 2025 Stockholm edition with 69.73 m) make him the clear favourite. Expect him to edge closer to 70 m again.

**Daniel Ståhl**, the Swedish home hero and reigning world champion (2025 Tokyo), will have the crowd behind him. The 33‑year‑old Olympic gold medallist (Tokyo 2020) threw **67.40 m** in Turku (2nd) and **69.01 m** at the Rehlingen meeting on 24 May. Ståhl’s championship pedigree is unmatched – he won the 2025 world title with 70.47 m – and he typically raises his level in Stockholm. However, he has not yet matched Čeh’s recent peak throws, and at 33 he may be slightly past his absolute prime. Still, a home‑soil boost and a solid 68.85 m are realistic.

**Matthew Denny** (29) is the Olympic bronze medallist from Paris 2024 and has shown explosive upside. In April he threw **74.04 m** and **73.58 m** in Oklahoma, results that dwarf the field’s seasonal bests. Yet his Diamond League form in May and early June has been more modest: a 2nd in Shaoxing (67.54 m) and a 3rd in Turku (67.26 m). Denny’s inconsistency between specialist throws meets and major DL stops suggests he may be peaking later. He remains a podium threat, but for Stockholm a mark around 68.12 m – slightly above his Turku performance – seems reasonable given his talent.

**Lawrence Okoye** (34) is the British record holder and a consistent 67‑m thrower. His 4th‑place finish in Turku (67.15 m) was his best of the year, and he also threw **71.88 m** in Oklahoma in April. At 34 he is experienced but no longer a 70‑m threat on a weekly basis. He should hold off the chasing pack with a 67.31 m effort.

**Roje Stona** (26), the Olympic gold medallist from Paris 2024, has had a mixed season. He threw **70.66 m** in Oklahoma in April but managed only 66.15 m in Turku (5th) and 64.92 m in Shaoxing. When Stona is on, he can beat anyone, but his recent inconsistency drops him to fifth. A mid‑66 throw is likely unless he finds an extra gear.

**Henrik Janssen** (27), the German champion and 2025 European Throwing Cup winner, had a strong late‑May block (68.54 m in Rehlingen, 68.47 m in Wiesbaden) but faded to 65.11 m in Turku. That volatility makes him hard to trust for a top‑five finish. Expect a rebound to the 66‑m range, but not enough to leapfrog Stona.

**Sam Mattis** (31) has struggled to replicate his 2025 best (71.27 m). His recent Diamond League outings have been in the low‑64s (64.83 m in Shaoxing), and he placed 7th in Turku? Actually he did not compete there. His 2026 best is 72.45 m in Oklahoma, but that was in an isolated meet. He is likely to settle for 64‑65 m, well off the leaders.

**Alex Rose** (34), the Samoan bronze medallist from the 2025 World Championships, has been hampered by a poor start to 2026. A 59.13 m in Shaoxing and a 68.17 m in Oklahoma (April) show his range, but the recent form is worrying. He will battle for eighth but is not a factor in the podium fight.

**Mario Alberto Díaz** (26) of Cuba is a 63‑65 m thrower at best on the international circuit. His 58.73 m in Shaoxing suggests he is still finding his feet at this level. A mark around 62.5 m is a fair projection.

**Head‑to‑Head Summary**  
The Turku meeting on 3 June (Čeh 69.13, Ståhl 67.40, Denny 67.26, Okoye 67.15, Stona 66.15, Janssen 65.11) provides the most direct cross‑comparison. Čeh’s dominance there, combined with his superior seasonal consistency, gives him the edge over the home favourite Ståhl. Denny’s huge April throws keep him in contention, but his recent DL form (67.26 in Turku, 67.54 in Shaoxing) suggests he is not yet at his peak. Okoye and Stona are closely matched, with Stona’s higher upside offset by his recent struggles. Janssen has the ability to upset but lacks reliability. The bottom three are clearly separated from the top six.

Stockholm’s atmosphere and a likely fair weather evening should produce a high‑quality contest, but Čeh’s current form and proven ability to win on the Diamond League stage make him the rightful favourite.

### Preview & Reasoning

This Stockholm field features the world’s finest steeplechasers, headlined by two-time Olympic champion **Soufiane el Bakkali**. His recent 7:57.25 in Rabat (31 May 2026) is the fastest time in the world this season and a full two seconds clear of the next best. That race demonstrated his superior water‑jump technique and finishing speed, making him the overwhelming favourite. Expect a controlled early pace before he surges between the last two barriers.

**Simon Kiprop Koech** (22) and **Edmund Serem** (18) both ran lifetime bests in that same Rabat race—7:59.44 and 8:01.61, respectively. Koech has been remarkably consistent over the past 18 months, with podium finishes in Xiamen, Brussels and the Kenyan Trials. Serem, the 2025 World bronze medallist, has already shown he can handle Diamond League pressure despite his youth. Their recent head‑to‑head confirms they are a tier below el Bakkali but clearly ahead of the chasing pack.

**Lamecha Girma** (25) is the world record holder (7:52.11) but arrives without a single steeplechase race in 2026. His last outing over the barriers was a disappointing 6th at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo (8:35.60), though he did win in Paris (8:07.01) earlier that season. His raw talent and proven ability to run sub‑8:00 mean he cannot be dismissed, but the lack of recent competition and his inconsistency at the global stage suggest he will settle for 4th, around 8:05–8:06. He should still outkick the next group.

The Moroccan **Salah Eddine ben Yazide** (22) ran 8:10.64 in Rabat (6th) and was 5th at the 2025 World Championships. He has a strong kick and has beaten many of today’s rivals in Monaco and Zürich. He edges out **Karl Bebendorf** (29), the defending Stockholm champion (8:11.81 here in 2025) and a consistent sub‑8:10 performer. Bebendorf’s 8:08.21 in Monaco last year and his familiarity with the Olympic Stadium’s rhythm give him an advantage over the similarly timed **Abrham Sime**. Sime clocked 8:14.09 on 3 June in Turku—respectable but a step behind his 2025 best of 8:07.92. The tighter turnaround may cost him a few tenths.

**Ruben Querinjean** (24)—the 2025 Diamond League winner in Brussels (8:09.47)—has the talent to challenge for top‑five, but he has not raced a steeplechase in 2026 yet. His winter indoor form (7:40.64 for 3000m) suggests good fitness, but the lack of barrier‑specific sharpness likely leaves him just outside the top six. **Daniel Arce** (33) and **Samuel Firewu** (21) both ran 8:11‑8:12 in Rabat, with Arce’s veteran savvy compensating for Firewu’s erratic recent form (12th in Rabat, DNF in Accra). **Abraham Kibiwot** (29) has an Olympic bronze medal but has not broken 8:10 since 2023; his 11th in Rabat (8:12.39) confirms he is no longer a podium threat.

**Ryuji Miura** (23) is the great unknown: he ran 8:03.43 in Monaco last year, but after a DNF in Hiroshima in April and no steeplechase since, his rhythm is suspect. A conservative 8:12‑8:13 seems realistic. **Geordie Beamish** (29) enters as the reigning world champion, yet his 8:16.80 in Rabat (13th) was a major disappointment. His winter indoor campaign (8:08.58 for 2 miles) hints at underlying endurance, but the steeplechase technique appears off. He should improve slightly in Stockholm but remains well off his 2025 title‑winning form.

The rest of the field is unlikely to threaten the leaders. **Kenneth Rooks** (26), the Olympic silver medallist, has been slowed by a 2026 season best of only 8:28.54. **Eisa Girma** (18) shows promise (8:23.59 in Brussels) but lacks the experience for a competitive Diamond League. Still, a sub‑8:10 race for the top six is on the cards.

### Event Preview & Analysis

The Oslo Diamond League is set for a blockbuster women’s shot put, bringing together the current world champion (Schilder), a two-time world outdoor champion (Jackson), and a two-time world indoor champion (Mitton) in what should be the deepest field of the 2026 season so far. The form lines from the early Diamond League circuit are incredibly telling, and the battle for the top spot looks like a two-woman war.

**1. Jessica Schilder (NED) – 20.82 m**
Schilder is entering this meet as the undeniable favorite. The 26-year-old Dutch thrower is in the form of her life. Her recent 21.09 m Dutch record in Shaoxing on 16 May was a statement, but it was her victory in Stockholm just three days ago (20.89 m) that really sets the tone for Oslo. She beat the entire top field there, including Chase Jackson. Schilder’s 2026 season has been marked by ruthless consistency and an ability to peak for the big moments—see her 20.69 m wins at the European Indoors and ISTAF Indoor Berlin. In Oslo, she will look to control the circle early, likely unleashing a huge second or third round to put the pressure on. Her only recent wobble was a 4th place at the World Indoor Championships in Torun, but she has clearly bounced back with a vengeance outdoors.

**2. Chase Jackson (USA) – 20.43 m**
Jackson, the 31-year-old American veteran, remains Schilder’s primary rival. She has an incredible resume as a two-time world champion, but the head-to-head data in 2026 heavily favors Schilder. Jackson won the World Indoor gold in Torun (20.14 m) and was impressive in Turku on 3 June (20.66 m), but she was decisively beaten by Schilder in both Shaoxing (20.46 m to 21.09 m) and Stockholm (19.91 m to 20.89 m). Her consistency in the 20.40–20.70 m range is world-class, but she hasn’t yet found the 21-meter gear that Schilder has unlocked. In Oslo, she will be desperate to close that gap. Expect a determined Jackson to throw over 20.40 m, but based on recent evidence, she will need Schilder to have an off day to take the win. Her victory in Stockholm last year over Schilder feels like a distant memory given the Dutch athlete's current trajectory.

**3. Sarah Mitton (CAN) – 19.92 m**
The Canadian champion is a model of consistency in the 19.80–20.40 m range. Mitton's peak this outdoor season came in Shaoxing (20.42 m for 3rd), and she has been the solid bronze medalist in the major Diamond League meetings (3rd in Turku, 3rd in Stockholm). At 29, she is a two-time World Indoor champion and a proven competitor, but she seems to be a clear tier below the Schilder/Jackson duopoly this year. Her main battle in Oslo will be to stay close to the leaders and fend off the chasing pack. She is unlikely to dip below 19.80 m and should secure a comfortable podium spot, but a jump into the 20.40s seems unlikely given she hasn't cracked 20.50 m outdoors this season.

**4. Fanny Roos (SWE) – 19.32 m**
The 30-year-old Swede is the clear "best of the rest." Roos has been remarkably consistent in 2026, placing 4th in Shaoxing (19.26 m) and 4th in Stockholm (18.90 m). She is a tough, experienced competitor who rarely has a bad day. While she doesn't have the raw power to challenge the top three, she has a strong technical base and will be highly motivated competing in Scandinavia. Her national record of 19.66 m shows her ceiling, but she hasn't hit that mark consistently this season. Expect a solid, professional performance around 19.30 m to hold off the German and Jamaican challengers.

**5. Yemisi Mabry (GER) – 19.01 m**
The Olympic champion from Paris 2024 has had a strangely subdued 2026 outdoor season. While she looked fearsome indoors—winning the German title with 20.37 m—her outdoor Diamond League form has been shaky. She placed 8th in Shaoxing (18.55 m) and 5th in Stockholm (18.79 m). This inconsistency is a major concern. At 27, she has the talent to challenge for a podium spot, but she hasn't put a full series together outdoors this year. Oslo represents a chance for a reset. If she can find her indoor rhythm, she could leapfrog Roos, but based on recent data, a #5 finish around 19.00 m is the most realistic prediction.

**6. Danniel Thomas-Dodd (JAM) – 18.84 m**
The veteran Jamaican, now 33, is still a very tough out. She is a former World Indoor silver medalist and has been hovering around the 19-meter mark all season (5th in Shaoxing with 19.12 m, 6th in Stockholm with 18.56 m). She is reliable and gritty, but her peak is likely behind her. She doesn't have the explosive speed to challenge the new generation of throwers. She should land in the 18.80–19.00 m range, which is solid but not enough to trouble the top four or five.

**7. Maggie Ewen (USA) – 18.52 m**
The 31-year-old American has had a difficult season. A 10th-place finish in Shaoxing (17.95 m) and an 8th in Stockholm (17.93 m) show a lack of form compared to her 2025 heights (where she threw 19.94 m). She failed to make the final at the 2025 World Championships (13th in qualifying). Her consistency has deserted her, and she appears to be in a rebuilding phase. Oslo will be a tough ask against this caliber of field.

**8. Jaida Ross (USA) – 18.35 m**
The 24-year-old Olympian is still developing at the senior level. She showed promise in 2025 (3rd at Prefontaine) but has struggled in 2026. Her 7th place in Shaoxing (18.79 m) was decent, but a 9th-place finish in Stockholm (17.80 m) was a step back. She is the youngest in the field and has massive potential, but she is still learning how to string together consistent results on the demanding Diamond League circuit. A finish near the bottom is expected, but she will gain invaluable experience.

### Reasoning and Analysis  

#### Top Contenders: Thea Lafond vs. Leyanis Pérez vs. Davisleydi Velazco  
**Thea Lafond** enters Oslo on a crest of outstanding form. At age 31, the Olympic and 2024 World Indoor champion has shown remarkable consistency in 2026: a wind-legal **14.84 m (−1.2)** at the Coqui Cup (17 May) and a **14.73 m (+0.1)** at Lucca just three days before this meeting. Her ability to deliver under pressure (silver at 2025 Worlds with **14.89 m**) and her recent string of 14.70+ legal jumps make her the most reliable candidate for victory. She has also proven she can win at the Bislett Stadion—she placed 5th here in 2025 but with a modest 14.26 m; this season she is a different jumper.  

**Leyanis Pérez** is the reigning World Champion (outdoor and indoor) and still only 23. However, her 2026 outdoor campaign has been quieter than her dominant indoor season (World Indoor gold with **14.95 m**). Her most recent outing, the Znamensky Memorial on 5 June, produced **14.59 m (−0.1)**—a solid but not spectacular mark. Pérez tends to peak for major championships later in the summer, but her raw talent and competitive DNA mean she cannot be counted out. She won the 2025 Oslo Diamond League with **14.72 m** and will be chasing a repeat. Still, Lafond’s higher recent peaks and consistent 14.80-level jumps give her a slight edge.  

**Davisleydi Velazco** (26) has been the revelation of the 2026 outdoor season. She has racked up a series of elite marks: **14.85 m (0.0)** at the Coqui Cup, **14.83 m (−0.2)** at Forbach, **14.71 m (+1.2)** at Filothei, and **14.64 m** in Tenerife. This consistency places her firmly in the 14.70–14.85 range. She also impressed in 2025 with **14.72 m** in Brussels and **14.65 m** in Zürich. Velazco is technically sound and appears to be peaking at exactly the right time. She could challenge for the win, but the experience and big-meet pedigree of Lafond and Pérez may edge her to third.  

#### Middle of the Pack: Saly Sarr, Liadagmis Povea, and Maja Åskag  
**Saly Sarr** (23) has progressed steadily. Her bronze at the 2026 World Indoor Championships (**14.70 m**) announced her arrival on the global stage. Outdoors, she won the African Championships with a wind-aided **14.79 m** and posted **14.57 m** (−0.6) at the Znamensky Memorial. While her legal best outdoors is still below 14.70, she has the momentum and youth to threaten the Cuban trio. A 14.62 m leap is a realistic improvement, placing her fourth.  

**Liadagmis Povea** (29) has struggled for consistency in 2026. After a modest indoor season (4th at Worlds with **14.41 m**), her outdoor marks have been underwhelming: **14.31 m** at the Cuban Championships and **14.19 m** (−0.3) at Znamensky. This is a far cry from her 2025 form when she leaped **14.84 m** in Brescia and **14.72 m** in Zürich. She may find a slight rebound in Oslo, but she appears to be a step behind the top three.  

**Maja Åskag** (23) is a dual-event jumper whose primary focus remains the long jump. Her triple jump in 2026 has been sporadic: a **14.24 m (+0.7)** at Filothei (3 June) is her best outdoor mark of the season—a promising sign. However, she has not broken 14.30 outdoors since 2025, and her indoor season included a poor 12.77 m in Dortmund. She is capable, but Oslo’s elite field will likely push her into the mid-14.20s.  

#### Bottom of the Field: Ackelia Smith and Ivana Španović  
**Ackelia Smith** (23) has not contested a triple jump since the 2025 season, where her best was **14.44 m** at the Jamaican Championships. In 2026, she has competed exclusively in the long jump, with only moderate success (best legal 6.81 m). Without recent triple jump competition, she is a major unknown and is unlikely to challenge the specialists. A **14.10 m** return would be a respectable effort.  

**Ivana Španović** (35) is a long jump legend dabbling in the triple jump. Her 2026 triple jump results are weak: a wind-legal **13.79 m** (−2.4) in Košice and a best indoor mark of **14.41 m** in January. At her age, she cannot match the depth of field here. Her focus is likely on the long jump later in the season, making a sub-14 m performance probable.  

### Conclusion  
The Oslo Diamond League triple jump shapes up as a three-way battle between Lafond, Pérez, and Velazco, with Lafond’s peak form and big-meet mentality giving her a razor-thin advantage. Sarr and Povea will fight for fourth, while Åskag, Smith, and Španović round out the order. The predicted marks reflect the athletes’ recent trajectories and the competitive pressure of a Diamond League setting.

### Race Preview & Reasoning

The Oslo Diamond League 400m is a rematch of the thrilling Rome Golden Gala from just six days earlier, where the top three finished within 0.20 seconds. That race provides the clearest form guide, but the home straight at Bislett Stadion, the presence of a deep field, and the differing trajectories of each athlete will reshape the order.

**Henriette Jæger** arrives as the in-form favourite. Her 49.60 victory in Rome – a season’s best and just 0.02 off her lifetime best – came after a dominant indoor season where she was second at Europeans and third at Worlds. She also ran 49.62 on this exact track in 2025, and the Norwegian crowd will lift her. Her ability to close strong (she split 49.74 to win the U23 title last summer) suggests she can dip under 49.6 again. Expect a slight improvement to **49.55**.

**Lurdes Gloria Manuel** is the reigning World Indoor champion (50.76 in Toruń) and at 20 has the highest ceiling in the field. She was runner-up to Jæger in Rome with 49.77, a personal best by a wide margin, and has been steadily lowering her marks since her indoor triumph. Her 200m speed (23.06 indoor this winter) gives her a lethal final surge. She lacks only the experience of closing out a Diamond League victory, but she will push Jæger hard. Prediction: **49.70**.

**Nickisha Pryce** is Jamaica’s national champion and a proven big‑race performer (NACAC champion, World finalist). Her Rome run of 49.80 was solid, but she has been inconsistent in 2026: she opened with 49.75 in Shaoxing, then slipped to 49.80 in Rome. Her 2025 season included a 49.63 in Monaco and a 49.46 semi at the World Championships, so the potential is there. However, she has struggled to translate that into back‑to‑back peak performances. In a tight field, she may lack the final‑gear edge of Jæger and Manuel. Prediction: **49.76**.

**Natalia Bukowiecka** is the most decorated athlete in the field (Olympic bronze, World silver, European champion) but her 2026 outdoor form is slightly below the top tier. She ran 50.12 to win in Bydgoszcz on 29 May – a good time, but a step behind the Rome trio. Her indoor season was excellent (World Indoor gold in 50.83, Polish record indoors), yet her outdoor races have not yet matched her 2025 peak (49.27 in the Tokyo final). She tends to improve through the summer, but at Oslo she may still be a tenth or two off. Prediction: **49.92**.

**Amber Anning** is the British record holder (49.29) and the 2025 World Indoor champion. However, her 2026 outdoor campaign has been shaky: she finished 5th in Rome (50.19) and has DNS’d several races. Her indoor season was mixed – she won the Arkansas twilight but was only 3rd at UK Indoors. She showed her class with a 49.36 at the 2025 World final, but she has yet to recapture that form this year. She may be race‑fit by Oslo but still lacks the sharpness of Jæger or Manuel. Prediction: **50.04**.

**Lieke Klaver** is a consistent championship performer (World and European relay golds, World Indoor silver in the 400m) but has never broken 49.8 outdoors. Her 50.62 in Rome was a season’s best but a clear distance behind the leaders. She ran 50.11 in Budapest last summer, so the speed is there, but she has not shown a significant uptick in 2026. Against this quality, she will struggle to move higher than sixth. Prediction: **50.38**.

The Norwegian duo **Josefine Tomine Eriksen Aks** and **Astri Ertzgaard** are respectable national‑level athletes but outclassed here. Aks’s best outdoor 400m in 2026 is 51.43 (Nairobi), and Ertzgaard’s is 52.37 (also Nairobi). ### Race Preview & Analysis

**The Headliner – Wanyonyi vs. Lutkenhaus vs. Arop**  
Oslo’s Bislett Stadion has historically rewarded front‑running speed and tactical brilliance, and this year’s field is loaded with sub‑1:43 talent. **Emmanuel Wanyonyi**, the reigning Olympic and World Champion, is the top seed. Though his 2026 season opener in Rabat (1:43.56) was a second slower than his 2025 Oslo win (1:42.78), Wanyonyi has a proven knack for rising to the occasion on this track. His 1:41.44 in Monaco last July and his World Championship victory (1:41.86) underline his class. He also has superior finishing power, as shown by his 1:41.95 in Stockholm in 2025.

**Cooper Lutkenhaus** arrives as the biggest threat. The 17‑year‑old world indoor champion (1:44.24) just ran a stunning 1:42.70 to win in Stockholm on 7 June, defeating Arop (1:43.11) and Bol (1:43.70). That performance, combined with his world U20 indoor record (1:44.03) and his raw speed (46.30 400m as a high‑schooler), suggests he can push Wanyonyi all the way. However, his inexperience in a deep, tactical Diamond League race may cost him the win by a few tenths as Wanyonyi’s race craft and closing speed edge him out.

**Marco Arop**, the 2023 world champion and North American record‑holder (1:41.20), is the most consistent 1:43‑1:42 performer on the circuit. His recent Stockholm run (1:43.11) shows he’s in strong form, but he has sometimes struggled to match Wanyonyi’s raw speed in fast, head‑to‑head affairs (e.g., 2025 World Championships: Wanyonyi 1:41.86, Arop 1:41.95). Expect Arop to run a controlled race and hold off the chasing pack for third.

**The Supporting Cast – Burgin, Tual, Bol, Crestan, English**  
**Max Burgin** has quietly built a superb 2026 campaign. He won in Rabat on 31 May with a sharp 1:42.98, beating Wanyonyi (1:43.56) and looking extremely comfortable. The British record‑holder (1:41.86 at age 20) has the strength to challenge the podium, but his lack of a truly sub‑1:42 this season (his best is 1:42.36 from 2025) puts him just outside the top three. **Gabriel Tual** is the European champion and has run 1:41.61 in his career, but his 2026 outdoor form (1:43.66 in Rome, 1:43.72 in Stockholm) is a step below the top trio. He is consistent and will likely lead the next group.

**Peter Bol** (31 years old) remains a perennial contender. His 1:43.70 in Stockholm was a solid season’s best, and his 1:42.55 in Monaco last summer proves he can mix it with the best. However, he typically fades slightly in the final 50 metres against younger legs. **Eliott Crestan** (Belgian record‑holder 1:42.43) is a master of indoor racing but has only run 1:44.08 outdoors this year; he lacks the top‑end speed to crack 1:43.4 here. **Mark English** (1:43.80 in Rome) is a gritty veteran but likely a place behind Crestan.

**The Strugglers – Attaoui, Grønstad, Sieradzki**  
**Mohamed Attaoui**’s 2026 outdoor season has been erratic. A brilliant 3:31.82 1500m in Turku on 3 June suggests great fitness, but his 800m effort in Stockholm just four days later (1:46.92) was a shocker. He may have been fatigued, but even a fresh Attaoui (PB 1:42.21) would need to rediscover his form to challenge the top eight in this field. **Tobias Grønstad**, the home favourite, has only managed 1:45.11 this season (Bruxelles, 23 May) and lacks the raw speed to compete with the 1:42‑1:43 specialists. **Patryk Sieradzki**’s history of DNFs in high‑level races (seven in 2025‑26) makes him a near‑certainty to pull up or finish last if he completes the race.

**Race Dynamics**  
With so many sub‑1:43 athletes, the first lap is likely to be quick – probably around 50.5‑50.8 seconds. Lutkenhaus and Arop will push the pace to test Wanyonyi’s endurance, while Burgin and Tual will sit just behind. Wanyonyi, as he often does, will position himself on the shoulder of the leaders and unleash his trademark kick off the final bend. Lutkenhaus may hold the lead into the straight, but Wanyonyi’s superior closing power (1:41.44 last year) will carry him home first. The final times will be fast but not record‑breaking, as the depth of the field prevents any single runner from stealing a runaway victory.

**Verdict**  
Wanyonyi reclaims his Oslo crown in a controlled 1:42.43, with Lutkenhaus rewriting the U20 record in a narrow second. Arop takes third, and the rest of the field spreads out behind a blistering early pace.

### Race Preview & Analysis

This is a deep and fascinating field. While an Ethiopian sweep of the top four looks likely – their recent form and physiological advantages over this distance are overwhelming – the battle for the minor places among a strong Australian contingent and several rising European talents should be compelling. The race is likely to be fast from the gun, as the Ethiopians, particularly **Freweyni Hailu** and **Likina Amebaw**, have demonstrated blistering early-season speed on the track. The only real question is whether anyone can stay with them.

#### The Favourite: Freweyni Hailu (ETH, 24)
**Why she wins:** Hailu is the reigning World Indoor 3000m champion (2025, Nanjing) and her recent outdoor form is impeccable. Just six days before Oslo, she ran a superb 14:18.94 in the 5000m at the Golden Gala in Rome (3rd place), showing she has fully transitioned from her indoor peak. Her indoor season was exceptional – an 8:19.98 in Liévin (a time that would be competitive in an outdoor race) followed by that World Indoor gold. Her 3:58.25 1500m win in Rabat in late May proves her raw speed is sharp. She has the best blend of raw endurance (from the 5000m) and searing speed (from the 1500m). On the fast Bislett track, she is the clear class of the field. Expect her to push a hard pace from 2000m to break the field, and her kick is lethal.

#### The Top Challengers
**Likina Amebaw (ETH, 28)** – **2nd.** Amebaw is arguably the form 5000m runner in the world right now, having dominated the Golden Gala in Rome on June 4th with a 14:18.41 victory. That is a huge statement. She also ran 14:24.21 in Shaoxing in May. Her 2025 season included a very strong 8:34.53 for 3000m in Chorzów, and she has shown remarkable consistency at high altitude on roads and cross country. The one concern is that her peak is very high over 5000m, and the 3000m might be *slightly* short for her to fully exploit her superior aerobic engine. She will not let Hailu get away easily, and a 14:18 5000m runner has the raw strength to run a very fast 3000m. She will push the pace hard and try to make it a gritty race.

**Hirut Meshesha (ETH, 24)** – **3rd.** Meshesha has a phenomenal 8:22.72 for the distance (Grand Slam Track Miami, May 2025), which is the fastest *outdoor* time in this field by a clear margin. However, her 2026 season has been inconsistent. She DNF'd a 5000m in May and has a best of 14:22.56 (6th in Rome), which is well off Amebaw's pace. Her 1500m speed is excellent (4:00.06 in Budapest in 2025), and she is a former World Indoor 1500m bronze medallist (2022). The question is whether she has the *current* form to match the very-best versions of Hailu and Amebaw. She will be in the mix, but her lack of a standout 2026 track performance suggests she may lack the final 200m kick to beat those two.

**Senayet Getachew (ETH, 20)** – **4th.** The young talent. Her 5th place in the Rome 5000m (14:22.37) was a huge breakthrough, and she has a 3rd place in Shaoxing (14:24.71) to back it up. She is more of a pure endurance athlete (World U20 5000m record holder indoors, strong half-marathoner) and is still raw. The 3000m is a step down in distance for her, which should favour her absolute speed. She has a huge engine and will be very tough to pass in the final laps, but may lack the final-turn kick to overhaul the more experienced trio ahead of her.

#### The Best of the Rest: The Australians and Europeans
**Linden Hall (AUS, 34)** – **5th.** The veteran Australian has been running the best 1500m of her career (3:56.33 in Brussels in 2025) and has a 8:27.03 indoor 3k from Boston this year. Her 14:40.81 in the Rome 5000m was a bit down, suggesting she’s better suited to the shorter distance. Her 1500m speed is a massive weapon here. She will sit just behind the Ethiopians and try to use her superior finishing kick. She should hold off the rest of the field comfortably.

**Hannah Nuttall (GBR, 28)** – **6th.** The British indoor and outdoor 5000m champion is a pure grinder. Her 8:32.94 indoor 3k at Millrose Games is a fantastic time, and she ran 8:44.74 in the Zürich Diamond League final last year. Her recent form includes a disappointing 9:04.20 in the World Indoor 3000m final, but her track record suggests she can rebound. She lacks the 1500m speed of Hall or Griffith, but her consistency over 3000m is excellent.

**Georgia Griffith (AUS, 29)** – **7th.** A World Indoor 1500m bronze medallist (2025) and Oceanian record holder over 3000m, Griffith has outstanding pedigree. Her 8:35.10 earlier in 2025 is a solid marker. However, her track record in 2026 has been less sharp: 4:18.18 for 1500m and 15:35 for 5000m at Australian Championships suggests she may be slightly off her absolute peak. She has great tactical nous but may lack the raw endurance to stay with the top 5.

Her 2026 form, however, has been quiet, with a 4th in the Australian 3000m and a modest 14:53 in Shaoxing. She has the talent to mix with the top Australians but needs a race to break through. She could surprise but more likely places in the second group.

**Maureen Koster (NED, 33)** – **9th.** The seasoned Dutch runner is a consistent performer, having run 8:33.47 indoors and 8:34.98 outdoors in 2025. Her 2026 outdoor form includes a 4:04.04 1500m and 14:33.56 5000m. She is a tough competitor who will run a very even race, but lacks the very top-end speed to challenge the leaders. She is a solid, reliable placer.

She has the raw speed and endurance, but her track racing experience is limited. This will be her first major Diamond League 3000m. The potential is massive, but the inexperience against a deep, fast field may see her fade slightly in the final stages. A future star.

Her outdoor best is 8:32.90 from Stockholm last year, but her 2026 form has been indoor-focused (8:40.92 in Karlsruhe). She has huge talent and guts, but expecting her to beat the seasoned pros in her first Diamond League 3000m as a senior is a step too far.

### Competition Preview & Analysis

**1. Ziyi Yan (CHN) – 69.52 m**  
There is simply no credible argument against Yan being the overwhelming favorite. At just 17 years old, she shattered the world U20 and Asian records with a **71.74 m** throw in Xiamen on 23 May 2026—a mark that is the second-best in history, behind only Barbora Špotáková’s world record. That performance was not an outlier; she has thrown **65.89 m**, **64.83 m**, and **64.55 m** multiple times in 2025, and her progression has been linear and explosive. In Oslo, she will face a competitive field, but her technical refinement and raw power at such a young age are unprecedented. Expect her to win comfortably, likely with a season’s best just short of 70 m, as the Oslo weather can be cool and windy, tempering absolute peak marks.

**2. Juleisy Angulo (ECU) – 65.88 m**  
Angulo is the reigning World Champion (Tokyo 2025, 65.12 m) and holds Ecuador’s national record. Her consistency is elite: she threw **63.25 m** in qualifying and **65.12 m** in the final at Worlds, and she has hit **62.33 m** and **62.25 m** in other meets. She is the most tactically sound thrower in the field behind Yan, with a proven ability to deliver under pressure. Her ceiling is not as high as Yan’s, but she is the clear second-best athlete here based on championship pedigree and recent form.

**3. Sigrid Borge (NOR) – 65.12 m**  
Borge will have the home crowd at Bislett Stadium, and she thrives in Oslo. She threw **65.00 m** in Xiamen (just behind Yan) and a huge **65.66 m** at the European Team Championships in 2025. Her personal best is only 63.28 m, but she has clearly elevated her game in 2025–2026. She is a five-time Norwegian champion and has shown she can handle the big stage, finishing 4th at Athletissima in 2025. The hometown advantage and her recent 65 m form put her ahead of the more decorated but slightly less explosive Sietiņa and Vilagoš.

**4. Anete Sietiņa (LAT) – 64.45 m**  
Sietiņa is the World Championships silver medallist (Tokyo 2025, 64.64 m) and a two-time Olympian. She is a model of consistency, rarely throwing below 61 m when it matters. Her **63.67 m** in qualifying at Worlds was a season’s best at the time, and she has multiple 61+ m throws in 2025. However, she has not yet broken 65 m outdoors in 2026, and her best marks are slightly below Borge’s recent peak. She is a safe bet for a top-5 finish, but she lacks the recent 65+ m sparks of the three ahead of her.

**5. Adriana Vilagoš (SRB) – 63.71 m**  
Vilagoš is the most talented thrower in the field after Yan, with a **67.22 m** win in Split in April 2025 and a **66.88 m** European Throwing Cup victory. However, her inconsistency is glaring: she finished 8th at the 2025 World Championships (61.29 m) and has had several mid-60 m throws followed by inexplicable 59 m or 58 m performances. In the 2026 season, she threw only 59.85 m in Nicosia and 59.22 m in Split before a decent 63.64 m in Xiamen. If she shows up focused, she could challenge for the podium, but her recent form suggests she is still rounding into peak shape. Fifth place is a fair assessment given the depth ahead.

**6. Elina Tzengko (GRE) – 62.34 m**  
Tzengko is the 2025 Diamond League champion and 2022 European champion, but her 2026 season has been a struggle. She threw only **55.96 m** in Xiamen (10th place) and **58.37 m** in Tokyo, a far cry from her 64.90 m win in Shaoxing in 2025. She is still young (23) and has the pedigree to bounce back, but her form in 2026 is worrying. She finished 5th at the 2025 Worlds (62.72 m) and has a win in Zurich (64.57 m) on her resume, but she seems to be in a technical slump. A mid-62 m throw is a reasonable expectation if she regains some rhythm.

**7. Flor Denis Ruiz Hurtado (COL) – 61.56 m**  
Ruiz is a veteran (34) with a World Championships silver medal (2023) and Olympic final appearances. She is reliable in the 60–62 m range, as seen by her **62.32 m** in the World Championships final and **62.11 m** in qualifying. However, she has not thrown beyond 62 m in 2026 (best: 61.76 m in Bogotá), and she finished 5th in Xiamen (60.84 m). The younger, more powerful throwers have overtaken her, but she remains a dangerous competitor who can steal a place if others falter.

**8. Nikola Ogrodníková (CZE) – 59.92 m**  
Ogrodníková is a two-time Olympian and bronze medallist from Paris 2024, but at 35, her best days are behind her. She threw only 59.87 m in June 2026 (her season’s best) and 53.54 m in May. Her personal best is 67.40 m from 2019, but she has not approached that level in years. She is a classy athlete who can still inspire, but she will struggle to compete with the current top tier.

**9. Marie-Therese Obst (NOR) – 58.77 m**  
Obst has been inconsistent: she threw 60.91 m in April 2025 but managed only a no-mark in Nicosia in March 2026 and a 57.52 m in the World Championships qualifying. She is a European bronze medallist (2024) and NCAA champion, but her peak performances are sporadic. In a stacked field, she will likely bring up the rear, though the home crowd might give her a slight boost.

**Key Storylines**  
- **Ziyi Yan’s historic trajectory**: At 17, she is already rewriting the record books. If she throws 70+ m again in Oslo, she will cement herself as the favorite for the 2027 World Championships and beyond.  
- **Angulo vs. Borge**: A battle between the reigning World Champion and the in-form Norwegian. Borge’s 65.00 m in Xiamen and home advantage make her a genuine podium threat.  
- **Vilagoš’s inconsistency**: Will the Serbian phenom string together two good throws in a row, or will she again falter after a promising start?  
- **Tzengko’s slump**: The Diamond League champion needs to reverse a worrying trend of sub-60 m throws in 2026.  

Oslo’s Bislett Stadium has historically produced dramatic javelin contests, but Yan’s dominance is likely to be the defining narrative. Expect a world-class competition with at least six athletes capable of 62+ m.
